# Reduce allocations in output formatter content negotiation

- [x] You've read the [Contributor Guide](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) and [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CODE-OF-CONDUCT.md).
- [x] You've included unit or integration tests for your change, where applicable.
- [x] You've included inline docs for your change, where applicable.
- [ ] There's an open issue for the PR that you are making. (Small perf change found in a perf survey, no issue.)

Remove small allocations from output formatter content negotiation

## Description

Every `ObjectResult`/`OkObjectResult` response goes through `DefaultOutputFormatterSelector`. This PR removes a few small allocations from that path.

- **`DefaultOutputFormatterSelector.GetAcceptableMediaTypes`**: return `Array.Empty` when there is no `Accept` header, so we no longer allocate a `List<MediaTypeSegmentWithQuality>` for it. When there is a header, the list is pre-sized from the number of comma-separated entries, so a single `application/json` no longer allocates a 4-element backing array.
- **`AcceptHeaderParser`**: add an internal `StringValues` overload so the header isn't boxed to `IList<string>`. The per-value parsing loop is shared with the existing overload and is unchanged.
- **`TextOutputFormatter.GetAcceptCharsetHeaderValues`**: return `Array.Empty` when there is no `Accept-Charset` header, which avoids boxing the `StringValues`.
- **`SelectFormatterNotUsingContentType` / `SelectFormatterUsingAnyAcceptableContentType`**: use indexed loops over `IList<IOutputFormatter>` and `MediaTypeCollection` instead of `foreach`, which boxed the enumerator.

No public API or behavior changes. Formatter selection order, sorting and the selected content type are the same.

### Results

I added `ObjectResultExecutorBenchmark`, which runs `ObjectResultExecutor.ExecuteAsync` with the HttpNoContent, String, Stream and SystemTextJson formatters. These are local BenchmarkDotNet runs (`--config profile`, 15 iterations) on a noisy 2-vCPU VM, with 3 interleaved A/B rounds. Each cell shows mean ± error.

| Accept | Round | Before | After | Allocated before → after |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| *(none)* | 1 | 787.9 ± 5.9 ns | 905.6 ± 19.3 ns | 712 B → **640 B** (−10.1%) |
| *(none)* | 2 | 875.4 ± 8.5 ns | 883.5 ± 28.5 ns | 712 B → **640 B** |
| *(none)* | 3 | 893.7 ± 24.0 ns | 870.2 ± 13.3 ns | 712 B → **640 B** |
| `application/json` | 1 | 1,196.5 ± 16.5 ns | 1,260.4 ± 14.1 ns | 792 B → **720 B** (−9.1%) |
| `application/json` | 2 | 1,229.0 ± 13.4 ns | 1,243.9 ± 13.2 ns | 792 B → **720 B** |
| `application/json` | 3 | 1,265.6 ± 10.1 ns | 1,237.2 ± 45.5 ns | 792 B → **720 B** |
| browser `text/html,...,*/*;q=0.8` | 1 | 1,683.4 ± 19.7 ns | 1,747.6 ± 18.5 ns | 832 B → **792 B** (−4.8%) |
| browser `text/html,...,*/*;q=0.8` | 2 | 1,693.0 ± 8.5 ns | 1,681.0 ± 15.6 ns | 832 B → **792 B** |
| browser `text/html,...,*/*;q=0.8` | 3 | 1,776.0 ± 49.0 ns | 1,699.1 ± 17.0 ns | 832 B → **792 B** |

The numbers are re-measured after the review feedback (bounded initial capacity; the benchmark now uses a fresh response body feature per invocation, which adds a constant ~216 B to both sides). Round 2 ran in reverse order (new first). Time is neutral within noise: round 1's base sample for the no-Accept case was an outlier that didn't reproduce.

Allocations drop by 40–72 B per response in every case. Time is neutral. Most of the remaining allocation comes from the benchmark harness (`StreamResponseBodyFeature`/`StreamPipeWriter`) and from `Utf8JsonWriter`, not from negotiation.

### Tests

- Added `AcceptHeaderParserTest` cases for the `StringValues` overload: multiple values, including empty and null entries, and `StringValues.Empty`.
- Added `DefaultOutputFormatterSelectorTest` cases for multiple `Accept` header values sorted by quality across values, and for an empty `Accept` header value.
- `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Core.Test`: 4514 passed, 0 failed, 3 skipped.

**🤖 Posted by ASP.NET Core Perf 2 (AI Agent)**
